prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned body of prose and poetry in Romanian that turns memory, the body and dream into an expansive metaphysical architecture.

statement.case_for: After reading the round-1 exchange and the chair's questions, my configuration does not change. My preference for Cărtărescu rests on the criteria of voice, formal achievement, sustained quality and imaginative depth. The test I apply is whether the voice is one I find in this writer's work and nowhere else. Public knowledge of the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid points to one long project: an interior cosmos built from memory, the body, the city and dream, carried by long, intricate sentences. His poetry belongs to the same project, so a citation can name prose and poetry together. His career spans decades and the late novels still look ambitious, which is the best available evidence on maturity. The case does not rest on nationality, fame or political symbolism, and it does not rest on the fact that Sem-Sandberg and I arrive at the same ranking. Agreement between two members is not evidence about the books. The chair's questions did sharpen where my confidence is limited. The Romanian original is the unresolved factor, and this ranking should be read as moderate confidence, not as settled.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still the one raised by Carlberg, Olsson, Palm, Swärd and Sem-Sandberg, and I raised it myself in round 1. Recurring imagery across very long novels may be repetition and not development. I cannot settle this from public knowledge and translations. If later volumes only re-stage earlier motifs, the sustained-quality claim weakens and Carson's case would be firmer. A second reservation is that I judge sentence-level density through translation, so some of what I credit as style may belong to the translator, and my claims about his poetry rest on thinner evidence than my claims about the major novels. Carson's case is real on voice and formal invention, and the scope objection to her is answerable. If her citation names only the original written work, as several colleagues propose, my doubt about hybrid and book-object forms mostly falls away. My remaining question about her is whether the mid-career and later books reach the level of Autobiography of Red and Nox. I cannot answer that from the supplied evidence.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Carson first and places Cărtărescu third. He says the real point of difference is repetition: a work built on recurring obsessions must show development and not only accumulation. He asks what the translated poetry and the earlier novels add, and he would test the Carson corpus mid-career book by book.
responses.response: I accept his framing of the repetition question and consider it the right test. I cannot resolve it from translations, and I will not claim to. My view is that the early novels and the poetry bear on it directly. If they show the same imaginative method working in other registers, the later recurrences look structural. If they show the same few gestures throughout, his objection holds. I also accept that Carson's variety of method is part of her claim and not evidence of unevenness. On the supplied evidence, the difference between us is where sustained quality is shown more securely. His view is that it lies in changing form across genres. Mine is that it lies in one long project whose scale I can see more of. I hold my view with moderate confidence.

responses.point: Palm ranks Carson first and Cărtărescu second. She says she can judge Carson's English directly but receives Cărtărescu's Romanian density through translation. She finds the risk of repetition more serious at Cărtărescu's scale than in Carson's shifting forms. She would turn to Cărtărescu or Robinson if the later Carson work cannot stand beside the landmark books.
responses.response: The translation asymmetry is real, and I have felt it in my own reading. I do not treat it as a reason to prefer the writer I can read directly, since linguistic access is not the same as literary merit. Swärd names the same risk of inflated confidence. Her fallback point interests me more. It suggests that the main open question for Carson is the later and mid-career work and not the landmark books. If that question were answered favorably, my ranking would be under more pressure. If it were answered unfavorably, her own route leads toward Cărtărescu. I agree it is the evidence to seek, and I have no way to supply it from the present record.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Carson first and keeps Cărtărescu as her first alternative. She would anchor Carson's citation in the original work (verse novel, poems, essays, Nox as elegy) and treat translations as evidence of engagement with antiquity. She admits uncertainty about how Romanian density survives translation and about possible repetition in his long novels.
responses.response: Her scoping of the citation is clear and defensible, and it answers my round-1 question about where achievement ends and scholarship or translation begins. I credit that answer. It leaves the maturity question where it was: whether the original work after the landmark books keeps up. I also notice that she and I share the same uncertainty about the Romanian from opposite sides. She treats it as a reason for caution about Cărtărescu. I treat it as a limit on what any of us can claim for him, which is not by itself an argument against him. For that reason I would not let the translation caveat decide the matter either way.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first. He argues that the repetition risk is the lesser one, because a recurring obsession can organize a body of work. He asks that it be tested against specific volumes. He is more doubtful than the others about Carson's hybrid and book-object works counting as literature within Nobel's will.
responses.response: I share his wish to test the repetition question volume by volume. I would resist his judgment that the risk is lesser. I do not yet have the evidence to rank the two risks, and treating his as smaller would be assuming what is in dispute. On Carson's hybrid forms I part from him slightly. If her citation rests on the written text, the contested genre labels become a question about method and not about eligibility. I would not count Carson's hybridity against her on that ground. My preference for Cărtărescu comes from the stronger evidence for a single developing project. It does not come from doubt about whether her work is literature.

responses.point: Swärd ranks Carson first and Cărtărescu second. She says Carson has changed instruments across verse novel, elegy, essay and drama, while Cărtărescu's case rests on recurring obsessions on a very large canvas. She says the translation asymmetry may inflate her confidence in Carson.
responses.response: I value her naming the asymmetry in her own judgment, because it is the kind of bias the whole committee should check in itself. I take her range-versus-depth contrast seriously. I answered it in round 1 by saying narrowness of motif is not narrowness of achievement unless the formal solutions stop changing. I still think that is right, but it puts the burden on volume-by-volume evidence, which none of us can supply here. If that evidence showed the late books repeating the early ones, her contrast would favor Carson. If it showed continuing formal discovery, her contrast would not settle the question. The committee should say plainly that this is the hinge.

uncertainties: My assessment of Cărtărescu relies on public knowledge and translations. The density of the Romanian original is only partly accessible to me, and I cannot verify translation quality across the long novels.
Translation coverage of his poetry and early prose is uncertain, so the poetry in the citation rests on thinner evidence than the novels.

I cannot settle whether the recurring motifs across the long novels are structural development or repetition. This is the largest single uncertainty in my configuration, and a volume-by-volume reading of the originals or the best translations could change my ranking.
I cannot judge from the supplied evidence whether Carson's mid-career and later books reach the level of Autobiography of Red and Nox, and her case depends on that.
I have not independently read the full corpus of any shortlisted writer, and my knowledge of later and shorter works is partial. I have not independently verified any source.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. None apparent from the supplied profile. The documented connections are ordinary collegial ones (shared committee service and the 2019 Academy renewal round), and none links to a shortlisted writer. My own practice as a historical and psychological novelist and critic is context and not evidence of preference. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
